answer: SR 26-2 supersedes SR letter 11-7, "Guidance on Model Risk Management" (April 4, 2011) and SR letter 21-8, "Interagency Statement on Model Risk Management for Bank Systems Supporting Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering Compliance" (April 9, 2021) [SR2602.htm p.1].
reference: SR 26-2 supersedes SR 11-7 (Guidance on Model Risk Management, 2011) and SR 21-8 (model risk management for BSA/AML systems).

answer: The revised model risk management guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets regulated by the Federal Reserve [SR2602.htm p.1].
reference: Banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets.

answer: Generative AI and agentic AI models are not within the scope of the revised model risk guidance [SR2602a1.pdf p.3]. The guidance applies to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models.
reference: No. Generative and agentic AI models are not within the scope; the principles apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models.

answer: SR 26-2 defines a model as a tool used in banking organizations to make decisions, forecasts, or assessments, and it emphasizes the importance of managing model risk through comprehensive documentation and validation processes [SR2602.htm p.1].
reference: A complex quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, or financial theories to process input data into quantitative estimates; it excludes simple arithmetic calculations and deterministic rule-based processes.

answer: The four factors that influence model risk under the revised guidance are the model's conceptual design and soundness, inputs, assumptions, and methodology [SR2602a1.pdf p.6].
reference: A model's inherent risk, exposure, purpose, and use.

answer: Model materiality is determined by model purpose and model exposure according to SR 26-2 [SR2602a1.pdf p.4].
reference: Model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality.

answer: Effective challenge refers to the critical analysis conducted by objective experts to evaluate model risk and implement necessary changes throughout the model lifecycle. The individuals performing effective challenge must have the appropriate expertise, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, and organizational standing and influence to effect any change [SR2602a1.pdf p.5].
reference: Critical analysis by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect changes across the model lifecycle; they need appropriate expertise, sufficient independence, and the organizational standing and influence to effect change.

answer: Model testing can include out-of-sample and out-of-time testing, comparison of alternative assumptions and methodologies, and a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs [SR2602a1.pdf p.6].
reference: Out-of-sample and out-of-time testing, comparison of alternative assumptions and methodologies, and a critical assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs.

answer: The components of model validation described in SR 26-2 include conceptual soundness, which involves assessing and documenting model design, construction, and developmental testing, as well as validating model limitations, errors, and appropriate use [SR2602a1.pdf p.8].
reference: Conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis, and ongoing model monitoring.

answer: Outcomes analysis can take forms such as testing during model development, ongoing monitoring reports, back-testing, or outlier analysis [SR2602a1.pdf p.9].
reference: Testing during model development, reports or analysis performed as part of ongoing monitoring, or standalone activities such as back-testing or outlier analysis.

answer: If a model no longer performs as expected, it may warrant overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment of the model depending on the banking organization’s model risk management policy [SR2602a1.pdf p.9].
reference: Overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment, depending on the organization's model risk management policy on model deterioration.

answer: Sound practice involves greater attention to the model’s limitations, informing stakeholders of those limitations, and determining appropriate controls when using a model before its validation is completed [SR2602a1.pdf p.8].
reference: Greater attention to the model's limitations, informing relevant stakeholders of those limitations, and appropriate controls such as limits on model use or closer performance monitoring.

answer: Internal audit's role in model risk management under SR 26-2 is to evaluate whether the model risk management practices are rigorous and effective and whether related policies are implemented accordingly [SR2602a1.pdf p.10].
reference: Internal audit generally does not duplicate model development or validation; it evaluates whether model risk management practices are rigorous and effective and whether policies are implemented.

answer: A bank should understand the conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance of a vendor model, as well as its accuracy, reliability, and fit for purpose [SR2602a1.pdf p.12]. Additionally, banks should validate vendor products, either internally or through external parties, and consider the limitations and assumptions of the model, especially when using vendor PDs as a proxy for default rates [SR2602a1.pdf p.11].
reference: Its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance, supported by ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis.

answer: SR 26-2 does not set forth enforceable standards; non-compliance will not result in supervisory criticism, but supervisory action may result for any violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices stemming from insufficient management of model risk [SR2602a1.pdf p.2].
reference: No. It does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements, and non-compliance will not result in supervisory criticism, although violations of law or unsafe practices can still lead to supervisory action.

answer: Adequate model documentation helps support effective model risk management by maximizing the likelihood of continuity of operations and assisting in model remediation efforts [SR2602a1.pdf p.11].
reference: Continuity of operations, tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions, and management of model remediation efforts.

answer: Under CECL, expected credit losses must be estimated over the entire contractual term of financial assets [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.6]. Prepayments and extensions are considered in the estimation process, and the methods used should reflect management's current expectations of credit losses.
reference: Over the contractual term considering expected prepayments; renewals, extensions, and modifications are excluded unless they are part of the original or modified contract and not unconditionally cancellable by the institution.

answer: Management must consider the effects of past events, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts on the collectibility of the institution’s financial assets when estimating the net amount expected to be collected [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.3].
reference: Past events, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts.

answer: ASC 326 requires reverting to historical loss information, or an appropriate proxy, for periods beyond the reasonable and supportable forecast period [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4].
reference: Reverting to historical loss information, or an appropriate proxy, for those periods (the reversion period).

answer: Yes, management may revert to historical loss information for each individual forecast input or based on the entire estimate of loss. This is stated in [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4].
reference: Yes. Management may revert for each individual forecast input or based on the entire estimate of loss.

answer: The acceptable reversion techniques under the interagency policy statement include immediate reversion, straight-line basis, or any systematic, rational method, as specified in [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4].
reference: Reversion may be immediate, straight-line, or use any systematic, rational method; no specific technique or reversion period is required.

answer: Management may use a loss-rate method, probability of default/loss given default (PD/LGD) method, roll-rate method, discounted cash flow method, a method that uses aging schedules, or another reasonable method to estimate expected credit losses [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.3].
reference: A loss-rate method, a probability of default/loss given default method, a roll-rate method, a discounted cash flow method, aging schedules, or another reasonable method.

answer: Examples of loss-rate methods under CECL include the weighted-average remaining maturity (WARM) method, vintage analysis, and the snapshot or open pool method [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.3].
reference: The weighted-average remaining maturity (WARM) method, vintage analysis, and the snapshot or open pool method.

answer: A collateral-dependent financial asset under ASC 326 is a financial asset for which the repayment is expected to be provided substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral when the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.5].
reference: An asset whose repayment is expected substantially through the operation or sale of the collateral when the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty as of the reporting date.

answer: The allowance for a collateral-dependent loan is measured using the fair value of the collateral for regulatory reporting purposes, regardless of whether foreclosure is probable [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.5]. The fair value of the collateral should be adjusted to consider estimated costs to sell if repayment depends on the sale of the collateral.
reference: Using the fair value of the collateral, regardless of whether foreclosure is probable, adjusted for estimated costs to sell where applicable.

answer: Yes, historical loss information can come from external data. The context states that historical loss information may be based on internal information, external information, or a combination of both [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4].
reference: Yes; it may be based on internal information, external information, or a combination, and may need adjustment for differences in current conditions.

answer: Historical loss information should be adjusted for differences in current asset specific characteristics such as underwriting standards, portfolio mix, or when historical asset terms do not reflect the contractual terms of the financial assets being evaluated as of the reporting date [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4]. Adjustments may be quantitative or qualitative and should reflect changes to relevant data such as unemployment rates or delinquency.
reference: Adjustments reflect how current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts differ from the historical loss period; they may be quantitative or qualitative and reflect changes such as unemployment rates or delinquency.

answer: The board should periodically review and approve written loss estimation policies, with the exact frequency not specified, but the validation process should be conducted regularly to ensure the process remains appropriate for the institution’s size, complexity, and risk profile [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.8].
reference: At least annually, as part of overseeing management's significant ACL judgments and estimates.

answer: ACL model validation activities include evaluating and concluding on the conceptual soundness of the model, performing ongoing monitoring activities, including process verification and benchmarking, and analyzing model output [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.10].
reference: Evaluating conceptual soundness including developmental evidence, ongoing monitoring including process verification and benchmarking, and analyzing model output.

answer: Yes, an institution may use multiple economic scenarios when estimating expected credit losses. [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.4] states that institutions are not precluded from considering multiple economic scenarios when estimating expected credit losses.
reference: Yes; institutions are not precluded from considering multiple economic scenarios.

answer: Purchased credit-deteriorated (PCD) assets are acquired financial assets that have experienced more-than-insignificant deterioration in credit quality since origination, as defined by FASB ASC Topic 326 [acl_policy_statement_2023.pdf p.5].
reference: Acquired financial assets that, at acquisition, have experienced more-than-insignificant deterioration in credit quality since origination.

answer: In the 2026 severely adverse scenario, the unemployment rate rises to a peak of 10 percent in the third quarter of 2027 [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.17].
reference: It rises 5.5 percentage points from 4.5 percent in 2025Q4 to a peak of 10 percent in the third quarter of 2027.

answer: In the 2026 severely adverse scenario, house prices fall by 30 percent, and commercial real estate prices decline by 39 percent [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.10].
reference: Nominal house prices fall 30 percent and commercial real estate prices fall 39 percent.

answer: In the 2026 severely adverse scenario, equity prices fall about 58 percent from the fourth quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026 [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.18].
reference: About 58 percent in the first three quarters of the scenario.

answer: The 2026 supervisory scenarios cover the period from the first quarter of 2026 through the first quarter of 2029, and each scenario includes 28 variables [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.13].
reference: From the first quarter of 2026 through the first quarter of 2029, with 28 variables in each scenario.

answer: In the 2026 baseline scenario, the unemployment rate moves up to 4.6 percent in the first quarter of 2026, stays at that level through the third quarter, and then gradually declines to 4.2 percent by the end of the scenario [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.14].
reference: It moves up to 4.6 percent in 2026Q1, stays there through 2026Q3, then gradually declines to 4.2 percent by the end of the scenario.

answer: No, the supervisory baseline scenario is not a forecast of the Federal Reserve. The document explicitly states, "These scenarios are not Federal Reserve forecasts" [2026_final_scenarios.pdf p.13].
reference: No; the baseline scenario is not a forecast of the Federal Reserve.

answer: Under the 2026 severely adverse scenario, the aggregate CET1 ratio declined from 12.8 percent to a minimum of 11.2 percent before rising to 12.7 percent at the end of nine quarters [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.17]. The 2026 stress test included 32 banks [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.31].
reference: For the 32 banks, it falls from an actual 12.8 percent in 2025Q4 to a projected minimum of 11.2 percent, then rises to 12.7 percent at the end of the horizon.

answer: Under the 2026 severely adverse scenario, the projected first-lien mortgage losses were $22.5 billion with a loss rate of 1.5 percent [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.27].
reference: Domestic first-lien mortgage losses of $22.5 billion, a portfolio loss rate of 1.5 percent.

answer: The total projected loan losses in the 2026 stress test were $625 billion, and the aggregate loan loss rate was 6.9 percent [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.26].
reference: $624.9 billion, a 6.9 percent loss rate.

answer: The projected credit card loss rate in the 2026 severely adverse scenario is 17.1 percent [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.27].
reference: 17.1 percent ($203.0 billion).

answer: The projected loan losses increased in the 2026 stress test due to greater loan losses resulting from an increase in loan balances and the severity of certain scenario variables, such as more severe changes in corporate bond spreads and commercial real estate prices [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.9].
reference: Loan balances grew by around 10 percent in 2025, concentrated in credit cards and wholesale loans, and some scenario variables were more severe, including corporate bond spreads and commercial real estate prices.

answer: The Board proposed averaging stress test results over two years to reduce the volatility of stress capital buffer requirements and increase transparency and public accountability of the stress test [2026_dfast_results.pdf p.7].
reference: To reduce the year-over-year volatility of stress capital buffer requirements.

answer: The Fed's First Lien Mortgage Model defines default as when a loan is 180 days or more past due, or if the loan status is marked as “real estate owned” (REO) or “involuntary liquidation” [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.106].
reference: 180 days or more past due, or a loan status of real estate owned (REO) or involuntary liquidation.

answer: The Fed's First Lien Mortgage PD model uses a loan-level, state transition approach, categorizing loans into four statuses (Default, Delinquent, Paid-off, Current) and estimating the probability of transitioning between these statuses based on loan characteristics, borrower attributes, and macroeconomic variables [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.133]. It projects probabilities of default and payoff for each loan, which are then used to calculate expected losses by multiplying PD, LGD, and EAD [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.204].
reference: A regression framework estimates quarterly transitions between payment statuses (current, delinquent, default, paid off) conditional on prior status, loan characteristics, and macro variables; default and paid off are terminal; separate models for ARMs and FRMs.

answer: The Fed's First Lien Model uses historical data on first lien payment status, loan losses, loan characteristics, and economic conditions, following an expected-loss framework that includes PD, LGD, and EAD components. This is detailed in [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.105].
reference: Loan-level data from the FR Y-14M report (Schedule A) and the supervisory scenarios, in an expected-loss framework with PD, LGD, and EAD components.

answer: The Fed's First Lien Model covers first lien mortgages secured by one-to-four family residential real estate in the United States, held for investment at amortized cost, excluding loans held for sale, commercial purpose loans, and non-portfolio loans [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.102].
reference: Portfolio loans only; the Board assumes no losses on government-program loans such as FHA or VA, and loans repurchased from the GSEs are included.

answer: The Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level sample dataset is constructed as a simple random sample of 50,000 loans selected from each full vintage year and a proportionate number from each partial vintage year [user_guide.pdf p.3]. Each vintage year includes one origination data file and one corresponding monthly performance data file [user_guide.pdf p.3].
reference: A simple random sample of 50,000 loans from each full vintage year and a proportionate number from each partial vintage year.

answer: The Estimated Loan-to-Value (ELTV) field in the Freddie Mac dataset is used to estimate the value of a property relative to the loan amount, and it is calculated using the appraisal value provided by the Seller. If the necessary information is not available, the ELTV may not be reported [faq.pdf p.7].
reference: Outstanding loan balance divided by the property's estimated current value from Freddie Mac's proprietary Automated Valuation Model.

answer: The codes in the Payment Deferral Flag indicate the period in which the payment deferral was granted. "C" stands for Current Period, and "P" stands for Prior Period [user_guide.pdf p.14].
reference: C means a payment deferral was granted in the current period; P means in a prior period.

answer: Data anomalies in the Freddie Mac loan-level dataset occur due to timing mismatches between default reporting cycles and investor reporting cycles, as well as seller/servicer reporting errors [faq.pdf p.3].
reference: Monthly performance and loss data combine elements from multiple reporting cycles and systems, so timing mismatches between default reporting and investor reporting cycles can appear as anomalies.

answer: The supervisory stress test scenarios use the national house price index, with state and county house price indexes aligning with the national macroeconomic path [fall_2026_credit_risk_models.pdf p.286].
reference: The Price Index for Owner-Occupied Real Estate from the Z.1 Financial Accounts of the United States (series FL075035243.Q divided by 1000).
